Improved_Statistics.Rmd

Introduction

This vignette shows the statistical methods added to ScreenR in version 1.15.4 and explains why they were added. It complements the vignette ScreenR Example Analysis, which shows the complete pipeline.

Topic New or changed functions
Design matrix and contrasts create_design_matrix(), create_contrast()
Significance of CAMERA and ROAST hits fdr and seed arguments, Log2FC column
Fold change of barcodes with zero reads pseudocount argument of compute_metrics()
Normalization method argument of normalize_data()
Gene-level Z-score test find_gene_zscore_hit()
Replicate-aware barcode statistics compute_barcode_statistics()
One model for the whole time course find_time_hit()
Combining the methods summarise_hits()
Quality control plot_replicate_correlation(), compute_gini(), find_discordant_barcodes() 
library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

Data

We use the example dataset of the package: an shRNA chemical lethality screen with 10 barcodes for most genes, two early time points (Time1 and Time2) and treated (TRT) and control (CTRL) samples in triplicate at two later time points (Time3 and Time4).

data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)

counts <- count_table
colnames(counts) <- c(
    "Barcode", "Time1", "Time2", "Time3_TRT_A", "Time3_TRT_B", "Time3_TRT_C",
    "Time3_CTRL_A", "Time3_CTRL_B", "Time3_CTRL_C",
    "Time4_TRT_A", "Time4_TRT_B", "Time4_TRT_C",
    "Time4_CTRL_A", "Time4_CTRL_B", "Time4_CTRL_C"
)
counts <- counts %>%
    mutate(Barcode = as.factor(Barcode)) %>%
    filter(Barcode != "*") %>%
    tibble()

groups <- factor(c(
    "T1/T2", "T1/T2",
    rep("Time3_TRT", 3), rep("Time3_CTRL", 3),
    rep("Time4_TRT", 3), rep("Time4_CTRL", 3)
))

object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts, annotation = annotation_table, groups = groups,
    replicates = ""
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
object <- normalize_data(object)
object <- compute_data_table(object)

Quality control

Replicate correlation

Replicates of the same condition should be more similar to each other than to the other samples. plot_replicate_correlation() shows the correlation of the log2 counts per million between all the pairs of samples.

plot_replicate_correlation(object)

Library evenness

The Gini index measures how unevenly the reads are spread over the barcodes: 0 means all the barcodes have the same number of reads, values close to 1 mean that a few barcodes take most of the reads. In a dropout screen it usually increases over time; a strong increase or a large difference between replicates can signal a bottleneck.

compute_gini() returns the values and plot_gini() plots them.

compute_gini(object)
#> # A tibble: 14 × 2
#>    Sample        Gini
#>    <fct>        <dbl>
#>  1 Time1        0.420
#>  2 Time2        0.434
#>  3 Time3_TRT_A  0.444
#>  4 Time3_TRT_B  0.445
#>  5 Time3_TRT_C  0.443
#>  6 Time3_CTRL_A 0.437
#>  7 Time3_CTRL_B 0.440
#>  8 Time3_CTRL_C 0.444
#>  9 Time4_TRT_A  0.477
#> 10 Time4_TRT_B  0.482
#> 11 Time4_TRT_C  0.482
#> 12 Time4_CTRL_A 0.470
#> 13 Time4_CTRL_B 0.466
#> 14 Time4_CTRL_C 0.471
plot_gini(object)

Normalization

By default normalize_data() divides by the total number of reads of each sample (method = "cpm"). When strong hits deplete a large part of the library, the total number of reads is a biased measure of the sequencing depth. method = "tmm" corrects it with the TMM normalization factors of edgeR, and method = "control" normalizes to a set of control barcodes (for example non-targeting shRNAs), when the library has them.

object_tmm <- normalize_data(object, method = "tmm")

# Ratio between the TMM and the total-count normalized values of each sample
# The normalized counts are the raw counts divided by the effective library
# sizes, so their ratio is the inverse ratio of the sizes
ratio <- get_normalization(object)$effective_library_size /
    get_normalization(object_tmm)$effective_library_size
tibble(Sample = names(ratio), TMM_over_CPM = round(ratio, 3))
#> # A tibble: 14 × 2
#>    Sample       TMM_over_CPM
#>    <chr>               <dbl>
#>  1 Time1               0.983
#>  2 Time2               0.997
#>  3 Time3_TRT_A         0.998
#>  4 Time3_TRT_B         0.987
#>  5 Time3_TRT_C         0.998
#>  6 Time3_CTRL_A        0.983
#>  7 Time3_CTRL_B        0.982
#>  8 Time3_CTRL_C        0.992
#>  9 Time4_TRT_A         1.01 
#> 10 Time4_TRT_B         1.02 
#> 11 Time4_TRT_C         1.02 
#> 12 Time4_CTRL_A        1.00 
#> 13 Time4_CTRL_B        1.01 
#> 14 Time4_CTRL_C        1.01

In this dataset the two methods agree within a few percent, so we keep the default.

Design matrix and contrasts

The edgeR/limma based methods need a design matrix and a contrast. A common pitfall is to rename the columns of model.matrix(~ groups): model.matrix() orders the columns alphabetically by group and the first group becomes the intercept, so renaming them in another order silently compares the wrong samples.

wrong <- model.matrix(~groups)
colnames(wrong) <- unique(groups)
# The column called "Time3_TRT" actually marks the Time3_CTRL samples
as.character(groups[wrong[, "Time3_TRT"] == 1])
#> [1] "Time3_CTRL" "Time3_CTRL" "Time3_CTRL"

create_design_matrix() creates a design matrix with one column for each group (no intercept) and create_contrast() creates the comparison between groups by name, which avoids this problem.

design <- create_design_matrix(object)
colnames(design)
#> [1] "T1.T2"      "Time3_CTRL" "Time3_TRT"  "Time4_CTRL" "Time4_TRT"

contrasts <- list(
    Time3 = create_contrast(design,
        treatment = "Time3_TRT", control = "Time3_CTRL"
    ),
    Time4 = create_contrast(design,
        treatment = "Time4_TRT", control = "Time4_CTRL"
    )
)
contrasts$Time4
#>      T1.T2 Time3_CTRL  Time3_TRT Time4_CTRL  Time4_TRT 
#>          0          0          0         -1          1

CAMERA and ROAST with a significance cut off

find_camera_hit() and find_roast_hit() now return only the genes with an FDR lower or equal to fdr (default 0.05) and report Log2FC, the median log2 fold change of the barcodes of each gene. Previously CAMERA returned all the genes with the requested direction (about half of the genes) and ROAST used the raw p-value.

The p-values are one-sided for the requested direction: camera and roast report two-sided p-values, which are twice too large for a test of depletion only. The FDR is computed from the one-sided p-values over all the genes, with the Benjamini-Hochberg method or, with fdr_method = "storey", with the less conservative Storey method when many genes have an effect.

ROAST uses random rotations: the seed argument makes the result reproducible, and its smallest p-value is 1 / (nrot + 1). method = "fry" uses limma::fry(), an exact and fast approximation of ROAST with continuous p-values. ROAST and fry are self-contained tests (does the gene change?), while CAMERA is competitive (does the gene change more than the others?) and becomes conservative when many genes have an effect.

camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrasts$Time4, fdr = 1)
roast <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrasts$Time4,
    nrot = 999, seed = 42, fdr = 1
)
fry <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrasts$Time4,
    method = "fry", fdr = 1
)

# Number of genes at different FDR levels
fdr_levels <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25)
tibble(
    FDR = fdr_levels,
    CAMERA = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(camera$FDR <= x), 1L),
    ROAST = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(roast$FDR <= x), 1L),
    fry = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(fry$FDR <= x), 1L)
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>     FDR CAMERA ROAST   fry
#>   <dbl>  <int> <int> <int>
#> 1  0.05      0     0     9
#> 2  0.1       3    11    12
#> 3  0.25      7    55    53

head(camera)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NGenes Direction   PValue    FDR Log2FC
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <fct>        <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173     10 Down      0.000214 0.0882 -0.515
#> 2 Gene_422     10 Down      0.000418 0.0882 -0.433
#> 3 Gene_296     10 Down      0.000495 0.0882 -0.508
#> 4 Gene_352     10 Down      0.00200  0.232  -0.467
#> 5 Gene_87      10 Down      0.00250  0.232  -0.436
#> 6 Gene_370     10 Down      0.00295  0.232  -0.344

The treatment effect in this example dataset is weak: at Time4 there are 0 genes at an FDR of 5% with CAMERA, 0 with ROAST and 9 with fry; at an FDR of 25% there are 7, 55 and 53.

A gene-level test for the Z-score

Why a new test

find_zscore_hit() calls a gene a hit when more than number_barcode of its barcodes have a Z-score below the median Z-score. By definition half of all barcodes are below the median, so for a gene without any effect the number of such barcodes is binomial with probability 0.5. With 10 barcodes and number_barcode = 6 the probability of being called a hit by chance is

pbinom(6, size = 10, prob = 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE)
#> [1] 0.171875

so about 17% of the genes without any effect are called hits.

The test

find_gene_zscore_hit() computes for each gene a score, the mean (or, with statistic = "median", the median) of the Z-scores of its barcodes, and compares it with the scores of many random sets of barcodes of the same size (n_permutations, default 100000). The p-value is the proportion of random sets with a score at least as extreme. This permutation test makes no assumption on the distribution of the Z-scores and gives continuous, well-calibrated p-values. The random barcodes are drawn from the whole library (default) or only from control genes (control_genes). Controls remove the true hits from the reference, but they must behave like genes without effect: in shRNA screens the non-targeting shRNAs often do not (targeting shRNAs are usually somewhat depleted compared with them), and in the K562 screen distributed with ScreenR they made hundreds of non-essential genes look like hits. Use them only after checking them, for example against known non-essential genes. The p-values are corrected with the Benjamini-Hochberg (or Storey) method.

The random sets of barcodes assume that the barcodes of a gene without effect behave like barcodes taken at random. They often vary together (similar knockdown, same region of the genome), so the scores of the genes without effect vary more than those of random sets: in the K562 screen, with the non-essential genes as controls, 20% of the other non-essential genes had a p-value below 0.05. reference = "empirical" compares the gene scores with an empirical null estimated from the centre of the distribution of the gene statistics instead, which includes this variation and is not widened by the hits; plot_empirical_null() shows the fit. In the benchmarks it kept the false positives at or below the nominal rate in the HAP1 CRISPR and K562 shRNA screens and, in the genome-wide HAP1 screen, found 90% of the core essential genes against 58% with the default reference.

The log2 fold changes are now computed with a pseudocount (compute_metrics(pseudocount = 0.5), in counts per million), so barcodes with zero reads in the treated samples get a finite fold change instead of about -23, which would distort the Z-scores of all the other barcodes.

metrics <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time4"
)
range(metrics$Log2FC)
#> [1] -4.384243  4.224517

gene_zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(metrics, fdr = 1, seed = 1)
head(gene_zscore)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NBarcodes  Score Log2FC     PValue     FDR
#>   <chr>        <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>      <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_364        12 -1.55  -0.473 0.00001000 0.00534
#> 2 Gene_296        10 -1.31  -0.499 0.000440   0.117  
#> 3 Gene_322        10 -1.13  -0.386 0.00159    0.283  
#> 4 Gene_419        10 -1.08  -0.311 0.00217    0.290  
#> 5 Gene_352        10 -1.02  -0.455 0.00326    0.348  
#> 6 Gene_422        10 -0.951 -0.430 0.00482    0.429

c(
    old_rule_hits = nrow(find_zscore_hit(metrics, number_barcode = 6)),
    gene_test_FDR_0.25 = sum(gene_zscore$FDR <= 0.25)
)
#>      old_rule_hits gene_test_FDR_0.25 
#>                 97                  2

Replicate-aware barcode statistics

compute_metrics() averages the replicates before computing the fold change, so a barcode that is noisy across replicates counts as much as a consistent one. compute_barcode_statistics() tests each barcode with the edgeR quasi-likelihood F-test, which uses the variability between replicates, and reports a signed Z-score that can be used with find_gene_zscore_hit().

barcode_statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(
    object, design, contrasts$Time4
)
head(barcode_statistics)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   Barcode Gene     Log2FC logCPM     F PValue   FDR Zscore
#>   <chr>   <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 10208   Gene_380  0.109   8.56 0.438 0.510  0.835  0.658
#> 2 10502   Gene_380 -0.480   4.97 0.748 0.390  0.765 -0.859
#> 3 10796   Gene_380 -0.665   6.61 2.49  0.120  0.515 -1.56 
#> 4 11089   Gene_380 -0.169   8.44 0.992 0.323  0.716 -0.988
#> 5 11382   Gene_380 -0.651   5.62 1.44  0.235  0.643 -1.19 
#> 6 11675   Gene_380 -0.286   9.66 6.71  0.0119 0.219 -2.51

gene_zscore_edger <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics, fdr = 1,
    seed = 1)
head(gene_zscore_edger)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NBarcodes Score Log2FC   PValue   FDR
#>   <chr>        <int> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173        10 -1.58 -0.521 0.000240 0.128
#> 2 Gene_422        10 -1.45 -0.451 0.000700 0.187
#> 3 Gene_15         10 -1.37 -0.321 0.00131  0.233
#> 4 Gene_296        10 -1.31 -0.493 0.00187  0.250
#> 5 Gene_370        10 -1.24 -0.394 0.00304  0.280
#> 6 Gene_168        10 -1.21 -0.256 0.00355  0.280
ggplot(barcode_statistics, aes(x = Log2FC, y = -log10(PValue))) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(
        x = "Barcode log2 fold change (Time4 TRT vs CTRL)",
        y = "-log10 p-value"
    )

One model for the whole time course

Analysing each time point separately answers “is there an effect at Time3?” and “is there an effect at Time4?”. find_time_hit() answers “does the effect of the treatment change over time?” with a single model, log(abundance) = a + b * time + d * treated + c * time * treated. The untreated and the treated samples each follow their own line over the time points (treated as equally spaced); c is the difference between the two slopes, i.e. how much the treatment effect changes per time point, and is 0 when the effect is constant. The coefficient c is tested for the barcodes of each gene with CAMERA. The early time points can be added as untreated baseline samples, so that the untreated line is estimated from four time points.

time_hit <- find_time_hit(object,
    treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL",
    baseline = c("Time1", "Time2"),
    days = c("Time1", "Time2", "Time3", "Time4"),
    fdr = 1
)
head(time_hit)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NGenes Direction      PValue       FDR Log2FC
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <fct>           <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_372     12 Down      0.000000157 0.0000836 -0.974
#> 2 Gene_296     10 Down      0.000000706 0.000135  -1.17 
#> 3 Gene_364     12 Down      0.000000760 0.000135  -1.01 
#> 4 Gene_412     10 Down      0.000112    0.0149    -0.815
#> 5 Gene_370     10 Down      0.000565    0.0604    -0.389
#> 6 Gene_349     10 Down      0.00376     0.318     -0.192

The column Log2FC is the median over the barcodes of the gene of c, the change of the treatment log2 fold change per time point. The top genes can be inspected with plot_trend().

plot_trend(object,
    genes = time_hit$Gene[1:2], group_var = c("Time1", "Time2", "TRT"),
    nrow = 1, ncol = 2
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Combining the methods

The overlap between the hits of the three methods can be shown with plot_common_hit(). Here each list contains the genes with an FDR of at most 25% (for the Z-score, the replicate-aware gene-level test).

alpha <- 0.25
plot_common_hit(
    hit_zscore = filter(gene_zscore_edger, FDR <= alpha),
    hit_camera = filter(camera, FDR <= alpha),
    hit_roast = filter(roast, FDR <= alpha),
    show_elements = FALSE, show_percentage = FALSE
)

find_common_hit() returns the genes in the intersection. summarise_hits() also shows how strongly each gene is supported: it puts the FDR of each method in one table and adds MaxFDR, the largest of them, which can be used as a conservative score to rank the genes supported by all the methods. Since an FDR is never smaller than the corresponding p-value, MaxFDR <= alpha means that the gene has a p-value of at most alpha in every method: for each single gene this is a level-alpha test, whatever the dependence between the methods. The list of genes with MaxFDR <= alpha does not, however, have a guaranteed false discovery rate, because the false discoveries of the single methods can concentrate in their intersection: treat it as a short list to validate.

summary <- summarise_hits(
    list(
        zscore = gene_zscore_edger, camera = camera,
        roast = roast, time = time_hit
    ),
    fdr = alpha
)
head(summary, 10)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 8
#>    Gene     FDR_zscore FDR_camera FDR_roast FDR_time NMethods MaxFDR Hit  
#>    <chr>         <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <lgl>
#>  1 Gene_296      0.250     0.0882    0.0534 0.000135        4  0.250 TRUE 
#>  2 Gene_370      0.280     0.232     0.111  0.0604          3  0.280 FALSE
#>  3 Gene_349      0.390     0.263     0.0668 0.318           1  0.390 FALSE
#>  4 Gene_352      0.280     0.232     0.157  0.508           2  0.508 FALSE
#>  5 Gene_87       0.280     0.232     0.207  0.508           2  0.508 FALSE
#>  6 Gene_422      0.187     0.0882    0.0534 0.545           3  0.545 FALSE
#>  7 Gene_412      0.590     0.306     0.0534 0.0149          2  0.590 FALSE
#>  8 Gene_325      0.649     0.738     0.0534 0.318           1  0.738 FALSE
#>  9 Gene_173      0.128     0.0882    0.0534 0.742           3  0.742 FALSE

In this dataset the genes with MaxFDR <= 0.25 are: Gene_296. The top gene of the time course model is Gene_372.

Discordant barcodes

A gene can be called a hit because of one or two barcodes with a strong effect, for example because of off-target effects. find_discordant_barcodes() reports the barcodes whose log2 fold change is more than threshold median absolute deviations away from the median of their gene.

discordant <- find_discordant_barcodes(metrics, threshold = 3)
nrow(discordant)
#> [1] 280
head(discordant)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   Barcode Gene     Log2FC GeneLog2FC Deviation
#>   <fct>   <chr>     <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>

#> 5 1033    Gene_358 -0.820    -0.0606     -13.5
#> 6 10318   Gene_21  -3.80      0.101      -12.1

# Discordant barcodes among the top genes
filter(discordant, Gene %in% head(summary$Gene, 10))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
